extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and observers of astronomy (late-19th/early-20th century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and inferential signs used to evaluate whether the dark markings on Mars (canals and oases) are vegetal and/or artificial, based on seasonal behavior, morphology, planetary physics, and analogy with terrestrial biology and engineering. Focus is on observational and logical standards an astronomer or informed layman would use to judge habitation and husbanding of water on Mars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetation explanation for the canals
rubrics_metrics.description: The canals are strips of vegetation fed by water from the polar caps; the floral seasons affecting the canals are conditioned indirectly upon the sun through its direct effect upon the polar snows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vegetal quickening would start where meltwater first reaches the surface and pass down the planet’s surface, producing the observed seasonal changes in visibility of the canals. This account explains both the timing and the manner of the canals' development and decline, and matches other observed traits (blue-green coloration, cartouche behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal timing: polar-melt-driven phenology (pole→equator) vs solar-driven (equator→pole)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Mars vegetation-timing follows the arrival of meltwater from polar caps (traveling from pole to equator), which is opposite to Earth where vegetal awakening follows the sun from equator toward pole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phenology curves (plots of dead-point of vegetation versus latitude/time) are bowed in opposite ways for Earth and Mars; this opposite direction of advance, visible in the curves and diagrams, is diagnostic of a moisture-controlled seasonal rhythm rather than a sun-controlled one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-source constraint: absence of permanent surface water; reliance on polar cap melt
rubrics_metrics.description: No permanent bodies of water stud Mars’ surface; the only surface water comes from the seasonal melting of the polar caps, so vegetation (if present) must wait for water to reach it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because water is spatially and temporally limited, vegetation would appear and disappear in patterns tied to the melt, producing the observed canal-season phenomena rather than patterns tied directly to solar return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartouche morphology indicating timed waning (northern zones dip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean cartouches in the polar, arctic, and sub-arctic zones dip down at their latter end instead of rising, indicating that the most northern canals were waning already by mid-August though others were not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dip denotes that canals in very north latitudes were 'snuffed out' prior to snowfall/frost; such gradual, preparatory extinction is exactly the behavior expected of vegetation adapted to its environment rather than abrupt mechanical obliteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local early activation of canals near polar edge (example: Jaxartes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some canals (notably the Jaxartes) show cartouches increasing apparently from the time observations began, consistent with early melting from the outer edge of the polar cap affecting nearby canals first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the cap melts from the outer edge inward, water liberated from outer parts can cause partial/local action before the main flow starts; the presence of such early-acting canals corroborates a polar-melt source hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-annual bipolar quickening evidenced by cartouche gradients
rubrics_metrics.description: The planet appears to have two seasons of vegetal growth—one quickened by the north polar cap, the other by the south—with evidence in cartouches where the previous semestral growth from the opposite pole is visible before the new impulse begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The slow fall to minimum followed by a sharper rise, and variations in pre-minimal gradients southward, are diagnostic: the temporal gradients and asymmetries tell which pole originated the prior impulse and how far its influence extended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between kinematic behavior and static appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinematic observations of the canals’ behavior over seasons corroborate what static images (appearance at rest) suggest about their nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flagstaff observations show that the changes in the canals over time (their dynamic behavior) reinforce the conclusions drawn from their momentary appearances; mutually corroborative static and kinematic testimony strengthens the vegetation/artificiality interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetation implies likelihood of fauna (flora→fauna inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because on Earth flora and fauna coexist throughout environments and are interdependent (plants as primary producers; animals as consumers and facilitators), the presence of a flora on Mars is a ground for suspecting animal life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments appeal to metabolic dependence, pollination, soil fauna (earthworms), and paleontological evidence of common ancestry; finding plant life makes it rational to look for animal life, though animal life may be harder to detect directly from afar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planetary mass/age as habitability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A planet must be sufficiently large to have achieved and retained the internal heat and atmosphere necessary for chemical evolution and liquid water; conversely, a planet's size influences its cooling rate and thus its effective biological age and the stage of evolution its biota may have reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large mass allows entrapment of heat and retention of atmosphere and water; secular cooling permits higher chemical complexity and the origin of life. Thus whether life exists, and its possible complexity, reduces to physical premises like size, atmosphere retention, and water availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Husbanding of water as motive for engineering canals
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the scarcity of water on an aging planet, intelligent inhabitants would be expected to construct lines of communication/engineering specifically to transport and manage water between polar caps and population centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The observed rectilineal canals and associated oases fit what one would expect if an intelligent species were 'husbanding' the planet’s diminishing water supply—i.e., purposeful channels connecting water sources and settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric regularity as evidence of artificial origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The rectilineal lines and roundish oases present an artificial-looking, geometric network analogous to centres and lines of communication; such geometricism is the primary visual trait suggesting handiwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overall artificial appearance, described as the 'cachet of an architect', is itself evidentiary: details that look like purposeful design (regularity, straightness, network structure) are exactly the sort of marks intelligence would leave and are unlikely under natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straightness of the canals
rubrics_metrics.description: The canals' pencil-like directness and apparent ruler-straight lines are a count in favor of artificial origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers note that nothing short of ruling could reproduce the precision seen; the straightness is emphasized as the trait that primarily strikes an unprejudiced observer and becomes more pronounced with better seeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual uniformity of canal size
rubrics_metrics.description: Each canal appears to be individually uniform in size (consistent width), which argues for planned, engineered construction rather than random natural features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity in dimensions across long distances is treated as anomalous for natural formations and supportive of an artificial explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme tenuity (very narrow width) of the canals
rubrics_metrics.description: The canals are extremely tenuous (very thin), a property cited as indicative of design rather than a natural broad feature like river valleys or belts of vegetation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The slenderness over planetary scales suggests constricted, controlled channels (e.g., for water transport) rather than diffuse natural phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual character of some canals (double lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some canals exhibit a dual character (appear as paired or doubled lines), which may indicate constructed conduits or paired works rather than single natural features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dual lines reinforce a notion of deliberate engineering (e.g., paired channels or embankments) and are anomalous under simple naturalistic interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position of canals with regard to the planet’s fundamental features
rubrics_metrics.description: The placement of canals relative to major planetary features (e.g., polar caps, latitudinal zones) is significant evidence—network positioning corresponds to needs such as water conveyance and settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their positions are not random but related to sources (polar caps) and sinks (oases/settlements), supporting the interpretation that canals are functional infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of canals to oases (canals as nerves and oases as ganglia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The canals relate spatially and functionally to the roundish oases, which look like ganglia (population or resource centers) to which the canals play the part of nerves (communication/transport arteries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This network morphology (lines connecting spots) mirrors what one would expect from centers of effort and lines of communication; the analogy strengthens inference of artificial coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the spots (oases) as centers
rubrics_metrics.description: The roundish spots (oases) have a character consistent with being centres of population or activity—distinct, localized, and playing a network role distinct from surrounding natural terrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their shape and relation to the canals (as termini or hubs) are treated as evidence that they function as organized centres analogous to settlements, agricultural hubs, or resource loci rather than mere natural lakes or patches.
